hints: Look at what atoms are in the backbone and side groups, especially chlorine, to judge both polymer type and disposal risk.
Count the carbons in the repeat unit. An addition homopolymer normally repeats just 2 carbons, so a 4-carbon repeat is a big clue.
Try splitting the 4-carbon unit into two 2-carbon alkenes to see if one or two monomers are needed, then test the named monomer in statement 3.
walkthrough:
**Identify the polymer type**

Look closely at the backbone. It is all C-C single bonds with no ester or amide link, so this is an addition polymer, not a condensation polymer.

Rule for addition:
$$\text{alkene monomer } \ce{C=C} \rightarrow \text{repeat unit } \ce{-C-C-}$$

**Check statement 1 about burning**

The repeat unit contains $\ce{C-Cl}$. Chlorine-containing polymers like PVC produce toxic $\ce{HCl}$ gas when burned.

$$\ce{-CH2-CHCl- + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + HCl}$$ 
So statement 1 is correct. Disposal by incineration is hazardous.

**Check statement 2 about one or two monomers**

A normal addition homopolymer repeat unit is 2 carbons long. Here the bracket shows 4 carbons: $\ce{-CH2-CHCl-CH2-CH(OH)-}$.

Split it into two 2-carbon pieces:
$$\ce{-CH2-CHCl-} \text{ from } \ce{CH2=CHCl} \text{ (chloroethene) }$$
$$\ce{-CH2-CH(OH)-} \text{ from } \ce{CH2=CHOH} \text{ (ethenol) }$$
That means it is a copolymer made from two different alkene monomers. So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 about the named monomer**

Statement 3 claims a single 4-carbon monomer, 3-chlorobut-2-ene-1-ol, $\ce{HO-CH2-CH=C(Cl)-CH3}$.

If that polymerised by addition, the double bond between C2 and C3 would open to give side groups $\ce{-CH2OH}$ and $\ce{-C(Cl)(CH3)-}$, which does not match the shown $\ce{-CHCl}$ and $\ce{-CH(OH)}$ pattern. It also contradicts statement 2. So statement 3 is incorrect.

Conclusion: 1 and 2 only are correct.

options.A: Correct. Statement 1 is true because Cl gives toxic HCl on combustion. Statement 2 is true because the 4-carbon addition repeat unit must come from two different ethene-type monomers, chloroethene and ethenol.
options.B: Incorrect. Although 1 is true, 3 is false. 3-chlorobut-2-ene-1-ol would not open to give the observed -CH2-CHCl-CH2-CH(OH)- sequence, and a single monomer cannot explain this copolymer pattern.
options.C: Incorrect. It correctly includes 1 but wrongly rejects 2. Many students miss that a 4-carbon addition repeat unit signals a copolymer of two 2-carbon alkenes, not a homopolymer.
options.D: Incorrect. It correctly includes 2 but wrongly rejects 1. Do not forget the environmental point: any polymer containing halogen produces toxic hydrogen halide gas when burned.
